newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Moscow still worried over Russians in Estonia.
newsitem.headline: Moscow still worried over Russians in Estonia.

text.p: Russia is still concerned over the rights of Russian-speakers in the Baltic state of Estonia although there are no gross human rights violations, a team of Russian experts said on Wednesday.
Moscow was infuriated with Estonia after it quit the former Soviet Union in 1991, introducing laws which have meant most Russian-speakers do not have citizenship.
Some 600,000 of Estonia's 1.5 million population are Russian-speakers but only a fraction are citizens.
The team of experts has just finished a trip to Estonia as it seeks to reassure Moscow over its Russians.
The visit was part of Estonia's efforts to wrap up a border deal with its huge neighbour, seen as vital as it seeks to gain entry into the European Union (EU) and NATO.

"I would not speak of massive and gross human rights violations but some human rights problems for the so-called Russian-speaking population surely exist," Vladimir Parshikov of the Russian Foreign Ministry's international and human rights department, told Reuters.
"The key problem is that tens of thousands of people simply cannot get citizenship of the country where they live," he said.
Estonian laws say people who arrived after 1940, the year it was annexed by the Soviet Union, have to apply for citizenship.
The thousands of mainly Russian-speakers who arrived during the Soviet era are regarded effectively as illegal immigrants and must undergo formal naturalisation.
One of the requirements for naturalisation is knowledge of Estonian, which many Russians do not speak, especially in the northest where some towns are more than 90 percent Russian.
